bc_upper_splitsville.blurb: Upper Splitsville is the higher sector of Splitsville, a crack-climbing crag in Murrin Park near Squamish. Nearly all of its two dozen routes are trad, mostly finger- to hand-sized splitters with a few off-widths mixed in. Grades run from 5.6 to 5.11, with the heaviest concentration in the 5.10 range and a handful of easier lines at 5.9 and below. A standard Squamish rack with doubles in the small to medium sizes covers most of it. The crag sits under old-growth forest, so much of the afternoon is shaded, which helps on hot summer days. The walk in is a real uphill hike, not a roadside crag.
bc_upper_splitsville.approach: From the Murrin Park parking lot, hike the Petgill Lake trail for roughly 20 to 30 minutes. The Upper sector is at the high end of the crag, on the left of the main trail.

bc_elusive_edge.blurb: Elusive Edge is an east-facing wall in the Southern Crags of Skaha Bluffs, above Skaha Lake near Penticton. Most of the 22 routes are bolted, with a handful needing gear. They run from the 5.8s through the 5.10s and 5.11s, with a few 5.12s on top, and the 5.10 range is the most common. Morning sun warms the face and it can stay lit later. The gneiss is mostly solid, although a few small holds have snapped off over the years. With plenty of mid-grade lines side by side, it works well for a group that wants a long day of volume rather than a single headline route.
bc_elusive_edge.approach: Follow the trail below the upper parking lot past the Daycare crags and the Diamondback sign. Where the trail splits several times, pass the left fork (to The Wave) and the right fork (to Raven's Castle), then climb up and leftward to reach the wall, which faces east.

bc_lower_talus_sector.blurb: Lower Talus Sector is a boulder field in the Hunter Creek area of the Fraser Valley, in the forest below a rockslide scar. Roughly two dozen problems sit on granite blocks scattered through talus, short and steep rather than tall. The grades lean toward the middle: most problems fall between V1 and V5, with a couple of easier ones and one far harder outlier. The ground is uneven and gets reshaped by freeze and thaw, so scrub holds, check for loose rock, and bring several pads plus sturdy shoes for scrambling between boulders. Getting around involves picking your own line over the rubble. It is the right fit for climbers who like a rugged session.

bc_upper_red_tail.blurb: Upper Red Tail is one of the Red Tail Group crags at Skaha Bluffs near Penticton, on the same hillside as Lower Red Tail and Another Buttress. Of its 21 routes, about three in five are bolted and the rest are trad. Grades are mostly 5.10 and 5.11, with the 5.11s the largest group and only a couple of easier or harder lines, so it is a good pick for strong intermediates. The group as a whole gets sun for most of the day, with lower walls partly shaded by trees, and a breeze tends to move through the valley. It is among the busier parts of Skaha because it sits close to the parking.

bc_another_buttress.blurb: Another Buttress is a popular crag in the Red Tail Group at Skaha Bluffs, near Penticton. It holds 21 routes, a blend of bolted lines and trad, with a few top-rope setups. Most of the climbing is easy to moderate, roughly 5.6 to 5.8, with a small number of harder pitches topping out in the 5.11 range. That makes it one of the better places at Skaha for newer leaders and for groups with mixed ability. The wall stays shaded for most of the day, so it is a sensible choice when the Okanagan summer sun is fierce. The rock here is the area's usual gneiss.

bc_backside_area.blurb: The Backside Area is a small zone behind the Papoose, a formation near Shannon Falls and the Stawamus Chief at Squamish. Most of its 21 routes are trad, with a few sport lines, mostly cracks and corners plus one slab and a roof crack. Difficulty is wide: the easiest climbs are around 5.6, the bulk fall between 5.6 and 5.10, and a few reach into the 5.11s and 5.12. Some routes are two pitches, so a 70 m rope helps. The wall gets morning sun and sits in shade by afternoon, so start early. The waterfall provides background noise instead of traffic, and the walk from the car is very short.
bc_backside_area.approach: From the car, follow the Papoose Descent trail for about five minutes, then take the left fork below Corner Unit. The Backside is roughly two more minutes along the base of the wall.
